perspective:
I am Mason Hurley, an accountant at a small community center. Martha Moua is my colleague, a personal care aide; we have a professional but not close relationship.

- I reviewed the community center’s financial reports and noticed discrepancies, especially unusually high healthcare expenses that did not match usual spending patterns. This made me suspect Martha might be mismanaging funds, and I felt suspicious and anxious.
- I asked Martha to discuss the report. I heard her say there might have been a misentry, and that she would review and correct any errors.
- After reviewing the report with Martha, I realized the discrepancies were due to a simple clerical error, not mismanagement. I felt relieved but embarrassed about my initial suspicion.
- I told Martha I appreciated her quick clarification. I apologized for suspecting her and said I should have asked her first. I heard her say errors happen, she understood I was being thorough, and we should double-check entries next time.
- I came to believe Martha was competent, but that the recurring clerical errors meant our financial management system was inadequate. I felt frustrated with the system and empathetic toward Martha.
- I told Martha the issue was not her management but the current system. I proposed creating a new, more robust financial system, said I would draft a proposal, and asked for her input. She agreed and offered to help address the gaps we identified.
- I finished drafting the new financial system proposal. I was hopeful about its benefits but uncertain whether management would approve or implement it.
- I told Martha about the draft. She called it solid, encouraged me to present it confidently, and said the benefits were clear. I said I would prepare a detailed presentation and asked her to help gather data to strengthen our case. She agreed.
- I presented the proposal to management. I felt satisfied with my efforts but physically and mentally exhausted. I believed I had done everything possible to advocate for the new system. Now the decision is up to management.
- I told Martha I thought the presentation went well. She said I did a fantastic job and suggested I take time off. I thanked her, said I would take a few days off to recharge and reflect, and hoped we would return to good news. She told me to enjoy the break and offered to help while I was away.
- I do not yet know management’s decision on the proposal.
